name: Henderson Far East Income Limited

valuation_approach.recommended_model: NAV-based model: project NAV-per-share forward using a component build of (i) revenue return per share less dividend per share (near-zero net retention after payout), plus (ii) an assumed long-run capital-return/NAV-appreciation rate for the underlying Asia-Pacific equity portfolio, then apply an exit premium/discount to NAV at a cost-of-equity discount rate. Do NOT build an FCF DCF.
valuation_approach.why_not_fcf_dcf: HFL.NZ/HFEL is a Jersey closed-end investment trust, not an operating company. Its Statement of Cash Flows records portfolio trading activity (sales/purchases of investments, loan drawdowns/repayments) rather than an operating business generating free cash flow; 'net cash inflow from operating activities' (£42.3m in FY2025) is portfolio income net of tax and working-capital moves, not FCF available to a claimant on an enterprise. There is no capex, no EBITDA, and no meaningful 'growth' concept analogous to an operating company's revenue/margin expansion.
valuation_approach.critical_flag_for_dcf_agent: Revenue return per share (24.98p FY2025) and dividend per share (24.90p FY2025) are within 0.1p of each other, so essentially ALL current income is distributed and the revenue reserve is barely built or barely drawn in a normal year (FY2025 drew only £1.5m/29,831k, i.e. ~0.8p/share from reserves). This means NAV growth cannot come from retained income compounding -- it must come almost entirely from capital appreciation of the underlying equity portfolio (or from accretive share issuance at a premium, which is NAV-additive but not organic). Any DCF/NAV model that assumes retained-earnings compounding on top of the full dividend will double count. Recommended build: NAV_t = NAV_(t-1) x (1 + assumed portfolio capital-return rate) + (small net revenue retention/deficit), with the terminal value computed as NAV_T x exit P/NAV multiple (use 0.95x-1.05x range; the trust has traded at a premium 8 of the last 10 years, average around 1.0-3.4%, but AIC-sector Asia Pacific Equity Income trusts more commonly trade at a discount, so do not assume the premium persists indefinitely). Discount at a cost of equity of roughly 9-10% (developed-market equity CoE plus an EM/Asia and small-cap-trust illiquidity premium; do NOT use WACC/FCF-style capital structure weighting since the 'debt' is a modest ~6-12% revolving credit facility used for short-term gearing, not permanent capital).
valuation_approach.historical_anchor_data: 10-year NAV/share history (31-Aug year-end): 2016 337.76p, 2017 375.19p, 2018 359.26p, 2019 358.99p, 2020 301.02p, 2021 299.58p, 2022 281.11p, 2023 222.12p, 2024 221.97p, 2025 223.32p -- a decline of roughly -4.5%/yr CAGR on a NAV-only basis. However NAV TOTAL RETURN (dividends reinvested) over the same horizon is +80.9% cumulative (10yr) per the FY2025 annual report performance table, i.e. a positive ~6.1%/yr compounded total return once the 10.8% annual cash yield is added back. Use total-return NAV compounding (not the bare NAV-per-share series) as the primary growth anchor, and present the bare NAV decline separately as the capital-erosion risk factor. H1-2026 (six months to 28 Feb 2026) shows a sharp NAV rebound: NAV total return +23.3%, NAV/share 261.38p, reflecting a strong Asian equity market including a >120% South Korea rally -- treat FY2026-to-date as a highly favourable, likely non-repeatable, six-month window rather than the new run-rate.

overview: Henderson Far East Income Limited (LSE: HFEL, NZX secondary listing: HFL) is a Jersey-incorporated, UK-tax-resident closed-end investment trust with roughly £408-519m of net assets, managed by Janus Henderson Investors (lead manager Sat Duhra, who became sole fund manager in mid-2024 after long-serving co-manager Mike Kerley retired). The trust holds a concentrated (~50-74 line, ~£433-537m) portfolio of Asia-Pacific-listed dividend-paying equities plus a modest covered-call/put option-writing overlay, with an investment objective of 'a growing total annual dividend per share, as well as capital appreciation.' HFL.NZ is a thinly traded NZD-denominated secondary listing of the same GBP-reporting vehicle, giving NZ investors unhedged GBP/NZD currency risk stacked on top of the trust's own unhedged multi-currency Asian equity exposure (the portfolio does not hedge its underlying AUD/TWD/KRW/HKD/SGD/INR/US$ exposures back to sterling).

business_model.summary: HFL is a pooled investment vehicle, not an operating company: it earns dividend/option-premium income (the 'revenue account') and capital gains/losses on its equity portfolio (the 'capital account'), and distributes income as a progressive quarterly (four interim) dividend. The trust must distribute at least 85% of annual investment income to retain UK investment-trust tax status (s.1158 Corporation Tax Act 2010). Since FY2023's strategic review, income capture and capital growth have been deliberately rebalanced: previously a 'deep value/high yield' style, the portfolio has shifted toward a blend of high-yield value names and higher-growth/lower-yield names (notably Korean and Taiwanese semiconductor and technology stocks) expected to grow dividends over time, using the option-writing programme to harvest additional premium income from these lower-yielding growth names without selling them outright.

revenue_streams.name: Portfolio dividend income
revenue_streams.trend: cyclical; FY2025 fell 11.1% as income normalised after an exceptional FY2024, H1-2026 investment income +90.8% YoY on large one-off dividends and a stronger market

revenue_streams.name: Option premium income (covered calls/puts written against portfolio holdings)
revenue_streams.trend: growing; used opportunistically to boost income from lower-yielding growth holdings, increased further in H1-2026 (+19-19% YoY) amid higher volatility

revenue_streams.name: Capital gains/(losses) on investment portfolio (non-recurring, market-driven)
revenue_streams.trend: highly volatile -- FY2023 capital return per share -56.35p, FY2024 -3.68p, FY2025 +1.42p (first positive capital return since 2017), H1-2026 +41.90p on a strong Asian equity rally

business_model.customer_type: Retail and wealth-adviser/platform shareholders in the UK (primary LSE listing, AIC 'Dividend Hero'-style income-seeking audience) plus a small NZ retail shareholder base via the NZX secondary listing seeking NZD-traded access to Asian dividend income
business_model.geographic_mix: Regional portfolio weight shifts materially year to year as the manager rotates: at 31 Aug 2025, China 29.9%, Taiwan 17.9%, South Korea 12.6%, Hong Kong 11.1%, Australia 9.0%, Singapore 7.2%, Indonesia 4.9%, India 4.5%, Thailand 1.1%, Philippines 1.0%, Japan 0.8%. By 28 Feb 2026 the mix had rotated sharply toward Korea (South Korea 24.2%, China down to 17.1%, Taiwan down to 12.3%, Singapore 11.4%, Hong Kong 10.1%, Australia 8.2%, Thailand 8.1%, Indonesia 5.5%, India 2.0%, Philippines 1.1%) reflecting the manager chasing a >120% South Korean 'value-up' corporate-reform-driven rally. Sector mix at 28 Feb 2026: Financials 35.1%, Technology 25.4% (Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, TSMC, MediaTek, Hon Hai all top-20 holdings), Consumer Discretionary 14.4%, Telecoms 6.3%, Real Estate 6.1%, Energy 4.3%, Industrials 4.1%, Basic Materials 2.4%, Utilities 1.9%. Reporting currency is GBP; the trust does not hedge underlying Asian-currency exposure back to sterling, and HFL.NZ holders bear a further unhedged GBP/NZD layer.

main_competitors: Schroder Asia Pacific / other AIC Asia Pacific sector trusts
Open-ended Asia-ex-Japan income funds and ETFs
competitive_position.market_position: One of the highest-yielding trusts in the AIC 'Asia Pacific Equity Income' sector (10.8% dividend yield at FY2025-end vs. Chairman's own statement of being '4.2% ahead of our closest peer'), and the only sector constituent to trade at a persistent premium to NAV rather than a discount through much of the past five years. However, per AIC sector data (7-Aug-2026), HFEL's share-price total return has trailed the Asia Pacific Equity Income sector average across every measured horizon (1yr 23.6% vs sector 40.7%; 3yr 50.5% vs 83.2%; 5yr 35.1% vs 72.6%; 10yr 72.1% vs 174.9%), indicating the very high income has structurally come at the cost of relative capital growth versus growth-tilted peers such as JPMorgan Asia Growth & Income.

moat_factors.description: Janus Henderson has managed the trust since 1992 and it is one of eight investment trusts run by JHI's dedicated investment-trust team; deep, on-the-ground Asia-Pacific coverage (~70 regional analysts) supports stock selection and access to management teams across ~10 markets.

18 consecutive years of dividend increases (to FY2025) and a headline 9-11% yield anchor a loyal income-seeking retail shareholder base that has kept the trust in persistent net share-issuance mode -- an unusual position in a sector where most peers trade at a discount and buy back shares.

moat_factors.factor: Premium rating enables accretive capital raising
moat_factors.description: Trading at a premium (3.4% at FY2025-end, ~3-5% through mid-2026) lets the Board issue new shares above NAV, growing net assets accretively (shares in issue rose from ~164.9m to ~182.5m in FY2025, and a further ~20.8m issued/planned in H1-2026, with net assets rising from £366m to £519m); this is a genuine structural advantage most discount-trading peers cannot use, and contributed to promotion to the FTSE 250 in April 2026.

moat_factors.factor: Options overlay as an income-generation tool
moat_factors.description: Writing covered calls/puts against individual holdings lets the manager extract income from lower-yielding, higher-growth names (e.g. TSMC, SK Hynix, SEA Limited) without needing to hold only high-dividend-payers, partially solving the income/growth tension inherent in an Asia income mandate -- but this caps upside participation in the names where calls are written.

0.75% flat management fee on net assets and no performance fee is reasonable but not a clear cost leader versus passive Asia-ex-Japan ETFs, and the 1.12% FY2025 ongoing charge has drifted up from a 0.97% FY2023 low.

weaknesses: Persistent multi-year share-price and NAV total-return underperformance versus both the AIC Asia Pacific Equity Income sector average and versus growth-oriented benchmarks (FTSE World Asia Pacific ex Japan, MSCI AC Asia Pacific ex Japan) across 1/3/5/10-year windows, reflecting the historic value/high-yield style missing tech-led rallies

Bare NAV-per-share has fallen from 337.76p (FY2016) to 223.32p (FY2025), a cumulative -34% / roughly -4.5% p.a. decline even before H1-2026's rebound, so a NZ or UK holder who has not reinvested dividends has seen meaningful capital erosion despite the headline yield

Dividend cover (revenue return per share vs dividend per share) has been close to or below 1.0x in several recent years (FY2023: 20.92p revenue return vs 24.20p dividend, a shortfall funded from the distributable reserve) -- the high yield is not fully self-funding from investment income alone in weaker years

Growing semiconductor/technology concentration (Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, TSMC, MediaTek, Hon Hai together a substantial share of the portfolio by early 2026) sits uneasily with a 'value/income' mandate and increases single-theme (AI capex cycle) risk that a pure income investor may not expect
Small, illiquid NZX secondary line versus the LSE-listed HFEL, meaning NZ holders likely face wider bid/ask spreads and less efficient price discovery

growth_drivers: Continued rebalancing from deep-value/high-yield toward a blended high-yield-plus-growth portfolio (post-FY2023 strategic review) aimed at restoring capital growth alongside income -- FY2025 delivered the first positive capital return per share (+1.42p) since 2017, and H1-2026 delivered a further sharp NAV rebound (+23.3% total return) as the rebalanced portfolio captured the Korean/Taiwanese tech and 'value-up' corporate-reform rally

Asia-wide corporate governance/dividend reform (Korea's 'value-up' programme, China's SOE shareholder-return push, Japan's decade-long reform, Singapore's new initiative) structurally increasing payout ratios and buyback activity across the region, a direct tailwind for a dividend-focused mandate

Structural secular themes cited by the manager: AI/semiconductor supply-chain leadership concentrated in Taiwan/Korea, financial inclusion in India/Indonesia/Philippines, renewable-energy/infrastructure build-out, and rising Asian middle-class consumption

Persistent share-price premium to NAV allows continued accretive share issuance (net assets grew from £366m to £519m within H1-2026 alone, aided by both market gains and new share proceeds), expanding the asset base, spreading fixed costs, and improving secondary-market liquidity (FTSE 250 entry April 2026)
Option-writing programme expansion during higher-volatility periods (H1-2026 option income +19% YoY) provides a second income lever that does not require chasing lower-quality high-yield stocks

business.description: Bare NAV per share fell from 337.76p to 223.32p over nine years (FY2016-FY2025) while the dividend was raised every year from 20.00p to 24.90p; dividend cover has dipped below 1.0x (FY2023) and the Company has explicitly drawn on distributable/revenue reserves to fund dividends in multiple years (FY2023 £2.875m from distributable reserve; FY2025 £1.5m from revenue reserve; H1-2026 £6.76m of revenue reserve plus £0.77m distributable reserve drawn even in a period of strong income). This is the central risk: a portion of the headline 9-11% yield has at times been effectively funded from capital/accumulated reserves rather than fresh income alone.

HFEL has trailed the AIC Asia Pacific Equity Income sector average NAV/share-price total return over 1/3/5/10 years (per AIC data to Aug-2026), and trailed its own comparator indices in 9 of the last 10 years; the FY2023 crisis (-13.0% NAV total return, capital-growth-driven Board strategic review and manager handover) shows the strategy can underperform materially in a weak year.

Portfolio rotated sharply toward South Korea (12.6% to 24.2% of the portfolio between Aug-2025 and Feb-2026) and technology (24.4% to 25.4%), driven by chasing the Samsung Electronics/SK Hynix/TSMC AI-memory rally; this increases exposure to a single macro theme (AI capex cycle, memory-chip pricing) and reduces the diversification benefit an 'income' trust is meant to offer versus concentrated tech vehicles.

Covered calls written against strongly performing growth names (TSMC, SK Hynix, MediaTek, Samsung Fire & Marine, DB Insurance etc.) mean the trust does not fully participate in rallies in those names beyond the strike price, a structural reason NAV can lag benchmark indices in strongly rising markets even when stock selection is sound.

Long-serving co-manager Mike Kerley retired from the industry in mid-2024, leaving Sat Duhra (co-manager since 2019, sole lead since) as the sole named fund manager of a ~£400-500m portfolio; while Duhra has 15 years at Janus Henderson, the loss of the second experienced voice removes a counterweight and concentrates key-person risk.

financial.description: The Company can borrow up to 30% of gross assets and drew £49.6m on its £50m revolving credit facility at FY2025-end (net debt/net assets ~6%, gross bank loans ~12% of net assets), rising further to fund H1-2026 investment; while modest in absolute terms, gearing magnifies both gains and losses in a market correction, and the facility (with RBSi, replacing SMBC) is renewed only every ~24 months (current facility expires Aug-2027), creating periodic refinancing/repricing risk.

financial.risk: GBP/NZD currency mismatch for NZX holders, on top of unhedged Asian-currency exposure
financial.description: HFL.NZ is NZD-quoted but the trust's NAV, dividends and reporting are GBP-denominated, with further underlying unhedged exposure to AUD, TWD, KRW, HKD, SGD, INR and other Asian currencies (the trust explicitly does not hedge). NZ holders therefore bear two full layers of unhedged currency translation risk on top of underlying equity market risk.

Written call/put options are carried as liabilities at fair value (£6.7m at FY2025-end, up from £1.0m the prior year) and are struck against individual stock price targets; a sharp adverse move in a name with an in-the-money written call can crystallise an opportunity cost or cash settlement obligation.

regulatory.risk: Loss of UK investment trust tax status
regulatory.description: The Company must distribute at least 85% of annual investment income and comply with s.1158 Corporation Tax Act 2010 to retain investment-trust status; a breach would expose realised capital gains within the portfolio to corporation tax, a material adverse outcome the Board and auditors treat as a standing compliance risk rather than an emerging one.

regulatory.risk: Dual UK FCA / Jersey JFSC / NZX regulatory regime
regulatory.description: The Company must simultaneously satisfy Jersey company/collective-investment-fund law, UK FCA Listing/Disclosure/Transparency Rules and NZX Listing Rules; incremental compliance cost and any divergence between regimes is a minor but persistent overhead versus a UK-only-listed peer.

regulatory.risk: NZ tax treatment of a foreign investment fund
regulatory.description: For NZ-resident holders, HFL.NZ shares in a Jersey-incorporated, UK-tax-resident closed-end fund may fall within NZ's Foreign Investment Fund (FIF) regime, under which NZ investors can be taxed on a deemed return (e.g. the 5% fair-dividend-rate method) rather than on actual dividends and capital gains, and UK-sourced dividends carry no NZ imputation credit benefit. This is a material structural consideration for NZ holders' after-tax yield and should be checked against individual circumstances with a tax adviser, not treated as investment advice.

macro.description: China remained the largest single country weight for most of FY2025 (29.9% at year-end, since reduced to 17.1% by Feb-2026); Chinese economic data, an ongoing weak property market, and reliance on SOE dividend-reform initiatives (capital market development, payout incentives) for the investment case leave the portfolio exposed to Chinese macro and policy surprises even as the manager has actively trimmed the weight.

A growing share of both portfolio value and recent performance is tied to the AI/memory-chip cycle (Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, TSMC); the Feb-2026 half-year report flagged a 'sharp sell-off in Asian software stocks' on AI-disruption fears and management explicitly expects 'more to come' as markets reassess AI cost-savings versus growth narratives.

macro.risk: Geopolitical shocks (Middle East conflict, US tariff policy)
macro.description: The H1-2026 chairman's statement flagged the Middle East war (oil price/Strait of Hormuz disruption, cut Western growth forecasts) and continued volatility from evolving US tariff policy (including a 2026 US Supreme Court ruling striking down major tariff programmes, creating both a refund opportunity and fresh uncertainty) as live macro overhangs for Asian markets and currencies.

A stronger US dollar has historically pressured Asian equities and currencies (noted explicitly in the FY2023 review); the trust's income is received in a wide range of unhedged Asian currencies, so USD/regional-FX and rate paths flow directly into both revenue and capital account volatility.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: IMF forecasts identify Asia as the fastest-growing global region (management's H1-2026 commentary cites ~60% of global growth in 2026), driven by AI/technology supply-chain leadership, financial-inclusion growth, infrastructure build-out and accelerating corporate governance reform in Korea, China, Japan and Singapore. Asian equities (MSCI AC Asia Pacific ex Japan) reached all-time highs by early 2026 and outperformed the S&P 500 for the first time since FY2017 in the year to Aug-2025, though the region remains volatile and sentiment-driven around China property/stimulus news, AI capex narratives and geopolitics (Middle East conflict, US tariff policy).
macro_factors.cyclicality: High -- as an ~fully-invested, modestly geared (roughly 6-12% net/gross gearing) Asia-Pacific equity portfolio, both NAV and dividend income are directly cyclical with regional equity markets, currencies and corporate payout decisions; option-writing dampens some volatility on the upside but not on the downside.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate -- Company borrowings are floating-rate (margin over SONIA or foreign-currency equivalent) via a revolving credit facility, so higher rates raise financing costs directly; more importantly, a stronger US dollar/higher-for-longer US rates have historically pressured Asian currencies and equity valuations, an indirect but material sensitivity flagged repeatedly by management.
key_input_costs: Investment management fee (0.75% flat on net assets, paid to Janus Henderson)
Finance costs on the £50m multi-currency revolving credit facility (RBSi, expires Aug-2027)
FX translation across ~9 Asian currencies (unhedged) plus a further GBP/NZD layer for NZX holders

recent_developments.event: NAV total return of 23.3% and share price total return of 22.9%, driven by a sharp rally in South Korean holdings (Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, Hyundai Motor, Kia Corp) amid the 'value-up' corporate reform programme and AI memory-chip demand; South Korea weight rose from 12.6% to 24.2% of the portfolio. NAV per share rose from 223.32p to 261.38p; net assets rose from £407.7m to £518.9m, aided by ~£39.1m of new share issuance (c.16m shares) plus a further £12.0m/4.8m shares post period-end. The trust was promoted to the FTSE 250 index in April 2026.

Sharp sell-off in Asian software/technology stocks as investors reassessed AI-driven business-model disruption risk; management flagged this as an ongoing theme likely to continue as organisations weigh AI cost-savings against growth, with the Middle East conflict (oil-price shock, Strait of Hormuz disruption) an additional near-term macro overhang cutting Western growth forecasts.

AGM held; all resolutions passed, including renewed share-buyback authority (up to 14.99% of issued capital) and non-pre-emptive share-allotment authority (up to 10% of issued capital) -- the latter reflecting continued expected premium-driven share issuance rather than buybacks, the reverse of most sector peers.

NAV total return +12.7% (vs FTSE World Asia Pacific ex Japan +14.1% and MSCI AC Asia Pacific ex Japan High Dividend Yield +13.9%); share price total return +13.6%; dividend raised to 24.90p (+1.2%, 18th consecutive year of increases), substantially covered by revenue with only £1.5m drawn from reserves; first positive capital return per share (+1.42p) since 2017; premium to NAV 3.4% at year-end, the only AIC Asia Pacific Equity Income sector constituent to trade at a premium; 17.6m new shares issued in the year raising £39.1m.

Board refreshment: Steven Wilderspin (Jersey-resident director, accounting/auditing background) joined the Board 5-Jun-2025; long-serving Senior Independent Director Julia Chapman retired 29-Oct-2025, succeeded by Carole Ferguson.

Fund management leadership passed from long-serving co-manager Mike Kerley (retired from the industry) to Sat Duhra, co-manager since 2019, following a Board-led strategic review after a difficult FY2023 (NAV total return -13.0%); the review explicitly rebalanced the portfolio from 'deep value high yield' toward a blend of income and growth names and stated the Company would draw on distributable reserves to supplement the dividend during the transition.

guidance.as_of: H1 FY2026 Half-Year Report (14 April 2026) and FY2025 Annual Report (10 November 2025)

items.target: Progressive/growing total annual dividend, four interim payments; two interim dividends of 6.25p each declared for FY2026 to date (+0.8% vs the equivalent prior-year interims)
items.notes: No numeric full-year FY2026 dividend target has been stated; the Board's stated approach is to fund dividends from current revenue where possible, add to the revenue reserve where possible, and use the distributable reserve to smooth payments in weaker years -- H1 FY2026 dividends were still partly reserve-funded (£6.76m revenue reserve + £0.77m distributable reserve drawn) despite very strong income growth in the period.

items.target: Continue issuing new shares at a premium to NAV to meet retail demand; EGM convened 14 May 2026 for additional non-pre-emptive share-allotment authority
items.vs_prior: increased -- demand and issuance pace both accelerated in H1 FY2026 (c.16m shares/£39.1m in six months vs 17.6m shares/£39.1m for the whole of FY2025)
items.notes: Management explicitly 'anticipate that demand will continue to be robust' and sought fresh shareholder authority beyond the AGM's standard 10% allotment limit, reflecting the trust's premium rating and FTSE 250 inclusion drawing in new demand.

items.target: No explicit numeric target; Board continues to permit borrowing up to 30% of gross assets via the £50m RBSi revolving credit facility, used flexibly for short-term/working-capital purposes rather than structural leverage
items.notes: £49.6m drawn at FY2025-end (~12% of net assets gross, ~6% net of cash); facility renewed with RBSi (replacing SMBC) shortly before FY2025-end, expires Aug-2027.

items.target: No explicit forward numeric target; FY2025 OCR was 1.12%, up from 1.08% (FY2024) and a 0.97% (FY2023) low
items.notes: Management fee remains a flat 0.75% of net assets; the OCR increase reflects other running costs rather than a fee-rate change.

guidance.management_commentary: Chairman Ronald Gould (H1 FY2026, 14 April 2026): flagged Middle East conflict-driven energy-price and growth-forecast risk as the dominant near-term macro overhang, while remaining confident in the underlying Asia investment strategy and portfolio positioning; noted the 2026 US Supreme Court ruling against major US tariff programmes as a source of both refund opportunity (>£200bn of 2025 tariffs potentially reclaimable) and fresh policy confusion. Fund Manager Sat Duhra (14 April 2026): reiterated that Asia's growth drivers (technology supply chains, financial inclusion, infrastructure, corporate reform) are broad-based and resilient, views the recent Asia-vs-US equity performance reversal as potentially the start of a longer-term re-rating, but explicitly flagged that AI-driven software disruption fears are likely to persist as a headwind for parts of the technology sector through the rest of FY2026.

bull_case: FY2023's strategic review and manager handover to Sat Duhra appear to be working: FY2025 delivered the first positive capital return per share since 2017, and H1-2026 delivered a 23.3% NAV total return, suggesting the rebalanced high-yield-plus-growth portfolio (with an options overlay) can participate more fully in Asian equity rallies while still paying a market-leading yield

One of very few investment trusts (in any sector) that trades at a persistent premium to NAV, letting the Board issue new shares accretively rather than buy back shares defensively -- net assets nearly doubled from around £362m (FY2023) to £519m (Feb-2026), improving liquidity, cost absorption and index inclusion (FTSE 250 from April 2026)

Structural regional tailwinds -- Korean 'value-up' corporate reform, Chinese SOE payout initiatives, Japanese-style governance reform spreading to more markets, and Asia's central role in AI/semiconductor supply chains -- are increasing both dividend payout ratios and earnings growth across the region, a genuine double tailwind for an income-and-growth mandate

Headline dividend yield (9-11%) is among the highest of any listed equity income trust and has grown for 18 consecutive years, providing NZ and UK income investors a differentiated, high-cash-flow access point to Asia-Pacific equities that most global or Asia-growth vehicles do not offer

10-year NAV TOTAL RETURN (dividends reinvested) of +80.9% to FY2025, improving further with the H1-2026 rally, shows that despite the alarming bare-NAV decline, a long-term holder who reinvested distributions has still compounded positive real returns, not simply eroded capital
bear_case: Bare NAV per share fell from 337.76p to 223.32p over nine years (FY2016-FY2025, roughly -4.5%/yr) while the dividend rose every year, and dividend cover has been at or below 1.0x in multiple years (FY2023 shortfall explicitly funded from the distributable reserve; FY2025 and H1-2026 both drew modestly on reserves too) -- for a shareholder who spends rather than reinvests the dividend, part of the 'income' has structurally been a return OF capital, not just a return ON capital

HFEL has trailed the AIC Asia Pacific Equity Income sector average on both NAV and share-price total return across 1/3/5/10-year windows (per Aug-2026 AIC data), and trailed its own comparator indices in 9 of the last 10 fiscal years -- the FY2023 crisis year (-13.0% NAV total return) shows how badly a value/income-tilted strategy can underperform when its style is out of favour

The post-2023 pivot toward Korean and Taiwanese semiconductor names (South Korea weight nearly doubling to 24.2% and Technology to 25.4% of the portfolio within six months) has traded one concentration risk (deep-value/high-yield underperformance) for another (AI capex-cycle and memory-chip pricing risk), and management itself flagged a February-2026 'sharp sell-off in Asian software stocks' as evidence the new risk is already live

The persistent share-price premium to NAV -- unusual in the sector and a genuine positive while it lasts -- is a market-sentiment phenomenon that could reverse; if HFL/HFEL were to move to a discount (as every other sector peer already trades), the accretive-issuance engine stops and the trust could instead face dilutive buyback pressure or NAV-negative discount-widening dynamics that most peers already contend with

For NZX-listed holders specifically: HFL.NZ is a small, comparatively illiquid secondary line versus the LSE-listed HFEL, quoted in NZD against GBP-denominated NAV and dividends (itself exposed to a further layer of unhedged Asian-currency risk), likely subject to NZ's FIF tax regime rather than favourable dividend/imputation treatment, and offers no natural hedge against a scenario where sterling strengthens against both the NZ dollar and Asian currencies simultaneously
